blocks.intro_md: Websites with open-access articles, written for a popular audience, with relatively high scholarly standards.

entries.name: Academy of Hebrew Language
entries.summary: Israel's official Hebrew-language academy; its website carries many scholarly articles on Hebrew linguistics across all periods.
entries.annotation_md:
- See above. Besides for a selection of scholarly articles from journals, has many articles specifically written for the website.
- Recommended. Focuses on Hebrew linguistics. Great resource, at a high level of scholarship, with lots of interesting articles on all topics related to Hebrew language, throughout history.
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_the_Hebrew_Language): “The Academy of the Hebrew Language was established by the Israeli government in 1953 as the "supreme institution for scholarship on the Hebrew language in the Hebrew University of Jerusalem of Givat Ram campus." Its stated aims are to assemble and research the Hebrew language in all its layers throughout the ages; to investigate the origin and development of the Hebrew tongue; and to direct the course of development of Hebrew, in all areas, including vocabulary, grammar, writing, spelling, and transliteration.”

entries.name: TheGemara.com
entries.summary: Edited English essays on the Babylonian Talmud, written for a general audience to academic standards.
entries.annotation_md:
- In English.
- Focuses on Talmud Bavli. Recommended. From the [About Us](https://thegemara.com/about): “We solicit original essays that are reviewed and edited by our in-house scholars, to ensure the highest academic standards as well as maximum readability for the general audience.”

entries.name: My Jewish Learning
entries.summary: Popular Jewish-education site with many good articles, mostly on Bible and modern Jewish history.
entries.annotation_md: - Lots of good articles. However, it mostly focuses on Bible and Modern Jewish history, which are out of the scope of this guide.

entries.name: 929- Tanach B’yachad
entries.summary: Modern Hebrew Bible-study site with many articles on Hebrew linguistics, though they are hard to filter out.
entries.annotation_md: - In Modern Hebrew. Lots of articles on Hebrew linguistics (for example: [on the phrase "עומד על הפרק"](https://www.929.org.il/page/528/post/12882)). However, mostly focuses on Bible, which is out of the scope of this guide. And not so simple to filter for articles on Hebrew linguistics.

blocks.intro_md:
Newspapers and magazines can be a great source of scholarship, and they’re often available online. They are especially good for reviews of scholarly books, and interviews with scholars.[^63] Israeli publications often have high-quality articles on Hebrew linguistics. Mostly behind paywall, with some articles not behind paywall.

Some of the best:

entries.name: Makor Rishon
entries.summary: Israeli Hebrew newspaper whose weekend Shabbat supplement often covers scholarly Jewish topics.
entries.annotation_md:
- In Modern Hebrew. Their [Mussaf Shabbat](https://www.makorrishon.co.il/tag/%D7%9E%D7%95%D7%A1%D7%A3-%D7%A9%D7%91%D7%AA/) (מוסף שבת) is especially good on scholarly topics.
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makor_Rishon):
  - “Makor Rishon is a semi-major Israeli newspaper [...] Shabbat (Sabbath) – a supplement for Jewish philosophy, Judaism and literature, with an intellectual bent.”

entries.name: Haaretz
entries.summary: Long-running Israeli daily in Hebrew and English; issues from 1918 to 1997 are in the National Library of Israel newspaper archive.
entries.annotation_md:
- In Modern Hebrew and English.[^64]
- Available online: 4 April 1918 - 31 December 1997 (22,721 issues; 394,984 pages), at National Library of Israel’s [Jpress archive](https://www.nli.org.il/en/newspapers/haretz/). However, not all pages in this date range are in fact available there.
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haaretz):
  - “Haaretz is an Israeli newspaper. It was founded in 1918, making it the longest running newspaper currently in print in Israel, and is now published in both Hebrew and English [...]”
footnotes_md: 64 Example of article on Hebrew linguistics, on the word “שחצן”: [המילה שַׁחְצָן: מה הקשר בין אריות לנחשים וביניהם לבין יוהרה?](https://www.haaretz.co.il/magazine/the-edge/mehasafa/.premium-1.2853618) https://www.haaretz.co.il/magazine/the-edge/mehasafa/.premium-1.2853618

entries.name: Segula
entries.summary: Israeli history magazine, monthly in Hebrew and bimonthly in English, since 2010.
entries.annotation_md:
- In Modern Hebrew and English.
- [Wikipedia - Hebrew](https://he.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D7%A1%D7%92%D7%95%D7%9C%D7%94_(%D7%9E%D7%92%D7%96%D7%99%D7%9F)):
  - “Segula is an Israeli monthly dedicated to history, published since April 2010. The magazine deals with the history of the people of Israel and general history, from the perspective that the people of Israel play an important part in world history and the historical processes leading humanity. The magazine is published monthly. An equivalent edition in English is published once every two months.”

entries.name: Tablet
entries.summary: Online magazine of Jewish news, ideas and culture, founded in 2009.
entries.annotation_md:
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablet_(magazine)):
  - “Tablet is an online religious magazine of news, ideas, and Jewish culture. Founded in 2009 [...]”.

entries.name: Jewish Review of Books
entries.summary: Quarterly magazine, launched in 2010, with reviews and essays on books and culture from a Jewish perspective.
entries.annotation_md:
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Review_of_Books):
  - “The Jewish Review of Books is a quarterly magazine with articles on literature, culture and current affairs from a Jewish perspective. [...] The magazine was launched in 2010 [...] ”

notes_md: 63 For an interesting example of newspaper interviews and lectures on YouTube being used as evidence in scholarly discussion, see Prof. Bezalel Bar-Kochva’s critique of Prof. Rachel Elior: [https://www.tau.ac.il/sites/tau.ac.il.en/files/media_server/imported/508/files/2014/10/elior-25.11.2013.pdf](https://www.tau.ac.il/sites/tau.ac.il.en/files/media_server/imported/508/files/2014/10/elior-25.11.2013.pdf). However, it must be admitted that that's an unusual case.

blocks.intro_md:
Blogs are generally not formally peer-reviewed and are generally written more informally and conversationally, but are often a great resource. With the shift from blogs to social media, many blogs have shifted to Facebook, and to a lesser extent Twitter and Reddit. (E.g., Mississippi Fred McDowel no longer posts on "On the Main Line", but does on Facebook.) Blogs are far less active than they were. There are a lot of Facebook groups, which I'm less familiar with, and technically have to be added to and aren't indexed by Google unfortunately (["walled gardens"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_platfor), vs. “open platforms”).

My focus here is on blogs with a substantial focus on academic/scholarly topics and style.

entries.name: The Seforim Blog
entries.summary: Long-running blog on Jewish books, bibliography and intellectual history, edited by Eliezer Brodt.
entries.annotation_md: Edited by Eliezer Brodt.

entries.name: The Talmud Blog

entries.annotation_md: Written by Natan Slifkin. Focuses on the relationship of science and Judaism, besides for contemporary politics and hashkafa.

entries.annotation_md: Founded by Shlomo Zuckier. Mostly articles related to contemporary issues, but many that have scholarly interest. Especially in section [Talmud and Halacha](https://thelehrhaus.com/talmud-and-halakhah/).

I recently received semicha from RIETS. This blog is devoted to parsha as well as whatever it is I am currently learning.”

blocks.intro_md:
YouTube has a lot of academic lectures. With the covid restrictions over the past two years, it has become especially common to live stream scholarly lectures (whether there’s a live component or not), and often the videos are then permanently publicly available on YouTube.[^66]

Some channels:

1. Academic lectures. Hundreds of lectures available. The YouTube channels seem to often be used now for live streaming of scholarly lectures:

entries.name: National Library of Israel (YouTube)
entries.summary: The National Library of Israel's YouTube channel of lectures and live streams.

entries.name: The Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities (YouTube)
entries.summary: YouTube channel of the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities, with recorded live-streamed lectures.
footnotes_md:
67 See here: [The Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities - YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/user/TheIsraelAcademy/featured) > “Past live streams”. Recent example that showed in my email inbox of youtube being used for live streaming of a scholarly lecture: [(PDF) 'Three Lectures on Habad Hasidism', Schocken Institute, Jerusalem, November 8, 15, 22, 2021 (Poser + Video) | Jonatan Meir - Academia.edu](https://www.academia.edu/59622961/_Three_Lectures_on_Habad_Hasidism_Schocken_Institute_Jerusalem_November_8_15_22_2021_Poser_Video_) When I was sent this link, Gmail even knew to attach the YouTube preview in the email.

The most extensive index I’ve found of open-access academic lectures online is the 90 (!) page list of links to lectures online (mostly YouTube) on Jewish mysticism compiled by Judy Barrett on her Academia.edu page: ["Best of the Web for the Zohar: lectures, interviews, conferences & courses (rev.5/11/20)"](https://www.academia.edu/38628191/Best_of_the_Web_for_the_Zohar_lectures_interviews_conferences_and_courses_rev_5_11_20_).

entries.name: Hebrew University (YouTube)
entries.summary: Hebrew University of Jerusalem's YouTube channel, an example of an Israeli university lecture channel.
entries.annotation_md: Israeli university channels. For example, Hebrew University ; Bar-Ilan University.

entries.name: Bar-Ilan University (YouTube)
entries.summary: Bar-Ilan University's YouTube channel, an example of an Israeli university lecture channel.
entries.annotation_md: Israeli university channels. For example, Hebrew University ; Bar-Ilan University.

entries.name: Yad Ben-Zvi (YouTube)
entries.summary: YouTube channel of Yad Ben-Zvi, a scholarly institute for the history of the Land of Israel.
entries.annotation_md: Scholarly organizations, such as Yad Ben-Zvi.

notes_md: 66 As for podcasts, many podcasts are also available on YouTube. For example, see below for the podcast “Channeling Jewish History”.

entries.name: Torah in Motion
entries.summary: YouTube channel with many lecture series, mostly on modern history, theology and Bible.
entries.annotation_md: A large number of lecture series. However, it mostly focuses on more modern history, contemporary theology, and on the Bible, so outside the scope of this guide. For lecture series within the scope of this guide, see for example the series with Dr. William Gewirtz, [The Changing Nature of Time in Halakha](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLGQrWlI7O--7uHNeabUKagPJ5vcjOVoUm), which is a four-part series that, according to the description, includes a lot of discussion of the history of the Jewish calendar.

entries.name: Seforim Chatter
entries.summary: Recommended podcast in which Nachi Weinstein interviews leading scholars about Jewish books and their research.
entries.annotation_md: Podcast hosted by Nachi Weinsten of Lakewood, NJ.[^68] Has interviews with top scholars discussing their most interesting research. For example, some previous guests include: Seforim Blog’s [Prof. Marc Shapiro](https://seforimchatter.buzzsprout.com/1218638/4566857-with-prof-marc-shapiro-discussing-his-books-rav-mazuz-rabbi-dr-yitzchak-isadore-twersky-and-more); [Jacob J. Schacter](https://seforimchatter.buzzsprout.com/1218638/4566965-with-rabbi-dr-jacob-j-schacter-discussing-rav-yaakov-emden-the-yaavetz), and many more. Recommended. Also has an associated [Twitter feed](https://twitter.com/SeforimChatter).[^69]
footnotes_md: 68 Introduction Show, Seforimchatter, [https://seforimchatter.buzzsprout.com/1218638/4587641-introduction-show](https://seforimchatter.buzzsprout.com/1218638/4587641-introduction-show), July 15, 2020, Season 1 Episode 18. (Accessed 13-Feb-22).

69 The tweets are also accessible at his website, and thus this can help one circumvent the need to sign up to Twitter as they can see all the tweets here without being signed up: [https://www.seforimchatter.com/tweets/](https://www.seforimchatter.com/tweets/) (pointed out to me by Nachi).

See the recent article about the podcast: Yosef Herz | APRIL 3, 2023, [One for the Books – Mishpacha Magazine](https://mishpacha.com/one-for-the-books-3/), about “Nachi Weinstein, the bibliophile behind the seforim chatter podcast”. See there this interesting quote: “I try to stay away from certain topics, namely academic Bible studies and academic dissections of Talmud and Chazal, because I don’t think they’re befitting a frum podcast.”

For an index of podcast episodes, see my article [“Index, by century discussed, of interviews of historians on Seforim Chatter podcast”](https://www.academia.edu/94100918/Index_by_century_discussed_of_interviews_of_historians_on_Seforim_Chatter_podcast).

entries.annotation_md: A number of discussions featuring R’ Dr. Eliezer Brodt “to briefly highlight some of the Rishonim and Acharonim ‘out there’ on this masechta”, see the latest Seforim Blog post [here,](https://seforimblog.com/2022/01/daf-yomi-seforim-on-moed-katan-part-one/) with links to previous.

For example, one episode is [an interview with Prof. Eric Lawee on a new book of his](https://youtu.be/8ey_9QBvv2w) on Rashi’s Commentary.

entries.summary: Podcast series of the Association for Jewish Studies.

blocks.intro_md: 10. Endless videos and podcasts, each of which must be judged on its own. One genre is well-edited videos with graphics by unknown hosts. Another type is podcast-type interviews with well-known personalities. A majority of all of these are focused on Bible, which as mentioned in the introduction, are outside the scope of this guide. Also, many of them are focused more on drawing lessons, in the “self-help” genre, and less on pure scholarship.[^71]
notes_md: 71 A few examples: R’ Dr. Ari Lamm’s podcast called [“Good Faith Effort”](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/good-faith-effort/id1536163226); Michael Eisenberg’s [YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCR6pKCe9d3jczqrMnOls4Pw/videos).
